claim: Pre-60S ribosomal particles are converted to translation-competent large ribosomal subunits during their final maturation in the cytoplasm.
source: During their final maturation in the cytoplasm, pre-60S ribosomal particles are converted to translation-competent large ribosomal subunits.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the general process of ribosome maturation, supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: eL40 recruitment stabilises helix 89 to form the uL16 binding site.
source: Single-particle cryo-EM reveals that eL40 recruitment stabilises helix 89 to form the uL16 binding site.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by cryo-EM structural data showing the interaction between eL40 and helix 89.

claim: The loading of uL16 unhooks helix 38 from Nmd3 to adopt its mature conformation.
source: The loading of uL16 unhooks helix 38 from Nmd3 to adopt its mature conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural observations showing conformational changes in helix 38 upon uL16 binding.

claim: Partial retraction of the L1 stalk is coupled to a conformational switch in Nmd3 that allows the uL16 P-site loop to fully accommodate into the PTC.
source: In turn, partial retraction of the L1 stalk is coupled to a conformational switch in Nmd3 that allows the uL16 P-site loop to fully accommodate into the PTC where it competes with Nmd3 for an overlapping binding site (base A2971).
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing the sequential conformational changes in the L1 stalk and Nmd3.

claim: The uL16 P-site loop competes with Nmd3 for an overlapping binding site at base A2971.
source: In turn, partial retraction of the L1 stalk is coupled to a conformational switch in Nmd3 that allows the uL16 P-site loop to fully accommodate into the PTC where it competes with Nmd3 for an overlapping binding site (base A2971).
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing overlapping binding sites for Nmd3 and uL16 at base A2971.

claim: The assembly of eukaryotic ribosomes involves the concerted action of over 200 trans-acting assembly factors.
source: The assembly of eukaryotic ribosomes involves the concerted action of over 200 trans-acting assembly factors.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about ribosome biogenesis.

claim: Pre-60S ribosomal subunits are exported to the cytoplasm following their assembly in the nucleus.
source: Following their assembly in the nucleus, pre-60S ribosomal subunits are exported to the cytoplasm where they are converted to translation-competent particles.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about ribosome biogenesis.

claim: The pre-60S particle attains export competence following release of the GTPase Nog2 by binding of the adaptor protein Nmd3.
source: The pre-60S particle attains export competence following release of the GTPase Nog2 by binding of the adaptor protein Nmd3 that recruits the nuclear export receptor Crm1 (Xpo1) through a C-terminal leucine-rich nuclear export signal sequence (Ho et al., 2000; Thomas and Kutay, 2003; Trotta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nmd3 recruits the nuclear export receptor Crm1 (Xpo1) through a C-terminal leucine-rich nuclear export signal sequence.
source: The pre-60S particle attains export competence following release of the GTPase Nog2 by binding of the adaptor protein Nmd3 that recruits the nuclear export receptor Crm1 (Xpo1) through a C-terminal leucine-rich nuclear export signal sequence (Ho et al., 2000; Thomas and Kutay, 2003; Trotta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Crm1-independent adaptors, including Arx1, Bud20, Mex67 and Ecm1 facilitate pre-60S nuclear export.
source: Crm1-independent adaptors, including Arx1 (Hung and Johnson, 2006; Bradatsch et al., 2007), Bud20 (Bassler et al., 2012), Mex67 (Yao et al., 2007) and Ecm1 (Yao et al., 2010) facilitate pre-60S nuclear export.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The AAA-ATPase Drg1 initiates the final cascade of cytoplasmic events by recycling the assembly factors Rlp24 and Nog1.
source: The AAA-ATPase Drg1 initiates the final cascade of cytoplasmic events by recycling the assembly factors Rlp24 and Nog1 (Kappel et al., 2012; Pertschy et al., 2007; Lo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Arx1-Alb1 heterodimer is bound at the end of the peptide exit tunnel.
source: The Arx1-Alb1 heterodimer is bound at the end of the peptide exit tunnel (Bradatsch et al., 2012; Leidig et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2016), from where it is released by the concerted action of the zinc-finger protein Rei1 and the cytosolic J protein Jjj1 (human DNAJC21) that stimulates the ATPase activity of the Hsp70 chaperone protein Ssa (Hung and Johnson, 2006; Lebreton et al., 2006; Demoinet et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2010; Lo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Arx1-Alb1 heterodimer is released by the concerted action of the zinc-finger protein Rei1 and the cytosolic J protein Jjj1 (human DNAJC21) that stimulates the ATPase activity of the Hsp70 chaperone protein Ssa.
source: The Arx1-Alb1 heterodimer is bound at the end of the peptide exit tunnel (Bradatsch et al., 2012; Leidig et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2016), from where it is released by the concerted action of the zinc-finger protein Rei1 and the cytosolic J protein Jjj1 (human DNAJC21) that stimulates the ATPase activity of the Hsp70 chaperone protein Ssa (Hung and Johnson, 2006; Lebreton et al., 2006; Demoinet et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2010; Lo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Incorporation of Rei1 requires prior release of Nog1.
source: Incorporation of Rei1 requires prior release of Nog1, whose C-terminal tail seals the exit tunnel as the particle transitions from the nucleolus to the cytoplasm (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Nog1's C-terminal tail seals the exit tunnel as the particle transitions from the nucleolus to the cytoplasm.
source: Incorporation of Rei1 requires prior release of Nog1, whose C-terminal tail seals the exit tunnel as the particle transitions from the nucleolus to the cytoplasm (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Rei1 inserts into the exit tunnel.
source: Interestingly, Rei1 also inserts into the exit tunnel (Greber et al., 2012; Greber et al., 2016) from where it is displaced during later cytoplasmic maturation steps by Reh1 (Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rei1 is displaced from the exit tunnel during later cytoplasmic maturation steps by Reh1.
source: Interestingly, Rei1 also inserts into the exit tunnel (Greber et al., 2012; Greber et al., 2016) from where it is displaced during later cytoplasmic maturation steps by Reh1 (Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A parallel branch of the cytoplasmic maturation pathway involves Yvh1-dependent exchange of uL10 for the placeholder protein Mrt4 to form the P-stalk.
source: A parallel branch of the cytoplasmic maturation pathway involves Yvh1-dependent exchange of uL10 for the placeholder protein Mrt4 to form the P-stalk (Kemmler et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2009; Rodríguez-Mateos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy has identified the binding sites for Nmd3 and Lsg1 on the intersubunit face of the 60S subunit.
source: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has identified the binding sites for Nmd3 and Lsg1 on the intersubunit face of the 60S subunit (Ma et al., 2017; Malyutin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nmd3 spans the tRNA corridor from the uL1 protein at the L1 stalk through the tRNA exit site and the PTC to interact with the anti-association factor eIF6 at the sarcin-ricin loop.
source: Nmd3 spans the tRNA corridor from the uL1 protein at the L1 stalk through the tRNA exit site and the PTC to interact with the anti-association factor eIF6 (yeast Tif6; herein called eIF6) at the sarcin-ricin loop (SRL), while Lsg1 embraces H69.
evidence: This is supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lsg1 embraces H69.
source: Nmd3 spans the tRNA corridor from the uL1 protein at the L1 stalk through the tRNA exit site and the PTC to interact with the anti-association factor eIF6 (yeast Tif6; herein called eIF6) at the sarcin-ricin loop (SRL), while Lsg1 embraces H69.
evidence: This is supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nmd3 release is dependent on the GTPase Lsg1 and the integration of ribosomal proteins eL40 and uL16.
source: The timing and mechanism of Nmd3 release remains unclear, but is dependent on the GTPase Lsg1 (Hedges et al., 2005) and the integration of ribosomal proteins eL40 (Fernández-Pevida et al., 2012) and uL16 (Hedges et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The eIF6 protein prevents premature joining of the ribosomal 60S and 40S subunits by binding to the SRL and ribosomal proteins uL14 and eL24.
source: The eIF6 protein prevents premature joining of the ribosomal 60S and 40S subunits by binding to the SRL and ribosomal proteins uL14 and eL24 (Gartmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Release of eIF6 in the cytoplasm is catalysed by EFL1 and its cofactor SBDS.
source: Release of eIF6 in the cytoplasm is catalysed by EFL1 (elongation factor like GTPase 1, an EF-2 homolog) and its cofactor SBDS (Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome, yeast Sdo1) (Bécam et al., 2001; Senger et al., 2001; Menne et al., 2007; Finch et al., 2011; Wong et al., 2011; Weis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The recruitment of SBDS to the 60S subunit depends on the prior integration of uL16 into the PTC in vivo.
source: The recruitment of SBDS to the 60S subunit depends on the prior integration of uL16 into the PTC in vivo (Weis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Recurrent somatic mutations in the RPL10 gene (encoding the ribosomal protein uL16) have been identified in 10% of cases of paediatric T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL).
source: For example, recurrent somatic mutations in the RPL10 gene (encoding the ribosomal protein uL16) have been identified in 10% of cases of paediatric T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) (De Keersmaecker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The T-ALL associated uL16-R98S missense variant impairs the release of both Nmd3 and eIF6.
source: The T-ALL associated uL16-R98S missense variant impairs the release of both Nmd3 and eIF6 (De Keersmaecker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Inherited mutations in the SBDS gene have been identified in 90% of individuals with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS).
source: Inherited mutations in the SBDS gene have been identified in 90% of individuals with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by poor growth, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, skeletal abnormalities and bone marrow failure with an increased risk of progression to myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) (Boocock et al., 2003; Warren, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SDS is associated with mutations in DNAJC21, the human homologue of yeast JJJ1.
source: SDS is also associated with mutations in DNAJC21, the human homologue of yeast JJJ1 (Dhanraj et al., 2017; Tummala et al., 2016; D'Amours et al., 2018) and EFL1 (Stepensky et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SDS is associated with mutations in EFL1.
source: SDS is also associated with mutations in DNAJC21, the human homologue of yeast JJJ1 (Dhanraj et al., 2017; Tummala et al., 2016; D'Amours et al., 2018) and EFL1 (Stepensky et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Immunoblotting revealed enrichment of the assembly factors Lsg1, Nmd3, Arx1 and eIF6 in the purified particles.
source: Immunoblotting revealed enrichment of the assembly factors Lsg1, Nmd3, Arx1 and eIF6 in the purified particles, but under-representation of ribosomal proteins uL16 and uL10 (P0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ribosomal proteins uL16 and uL10 (P0) were under-represented in the purified particles.
source: Immunoblotting revealed enrichment of the assembly factors Lsg1, Nmd3, Arx1 and eIF6 in the purified particles, but under-representation of ribosomal proteins uL16 and uL10 (P0) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Analysis by single-particle cryo-EM with extensive 3D classification yielded a series of structures (states I-VI) that likely reflect sequential snapshots of final cytoplasmic pre-60S maturation.
source: Analysis by single-particle cryo-EM with extensive 3D classification yielded a series of structures (hereafter termed states I-VI) that likely reflect sequential snapshots of final cytoplasmic pre-60S maturation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and classification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All six pre-60S cryo-EM reconstructions were refined to average resolutions of 3.1–3.9 Å with the local resolution extending to 2.3 Å in the core of the particles in states I and III.
source: We refined all six pre-60S cryo-EM reconstructions to average resolutions of 3.1–3.9 Å with the local resolution extending to 2.3 Å in the core of the particles in states I and III (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by the resolution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Density corresponding to the phosphatase and zinc finger domains of Yvh1 was identified situated between uL11 in the P-stalk and eIF6.
source: In addition, we identified density corresponding to the phosphatase (Baßler et al., 2017) and zinc finger (Zhou et al., 2019) domains of Yvh1 situated between uL11 in the P-stalk and eIF6 (Figure 1A, states I-II).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 1A, states I-II.

claim: Sequential maturation of the cytoplasmic pre-60S subunit couples dramatic conformational rearrangements of two long flexible helices (the L1 stalk and H38) to recruitment of the final ribosomal proteins (eL40 and uL16) and assembly factor displacement.
source: Sequential maturation of the cytoplasmic pre-60S subunit couples dramatic conformational rearrangements of two long flexible helices (the L1 stalk and H38) to recruitment of the final ribosomal proteins (eL40 and uL16) and assembly factor displacement (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In states I-III, the L1 stalk is displaced inwards with H38 in the 'closed' position.
source: In states I-III, the L1 stalk is displaced inwards with H38 in the 'closed' position.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Rearrangement of H38 to the mature position (state IV) is followed by partial (state V) then full (state VI) retraction of the L1 stalk.
source: Rearrangement of H38 to the mature position (state IV) is followed by partial (state V) then full (state VI) retraction of the L1 stalk.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Yvh1 is predominantly bound in state I, is present at low occupancy in state II but is absent in state III.
source: Focused classification around the P-stalk revealed that Yvh1 is predominantly bound in state I, is present at low occupancy in state II but is absent in state III.
evidence: This is supported by focused classification of the cryo-EM data.

claim: Yvh1 and eL40 do not appear to bind simultaneously to the same particle.
source: Thus, Yvh1 and eL40 do not appear to bind simultaneously to the same particle.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing mutually exclusive binding.

claim: The homologous C-termini of Reh1 and Rei1 occupy the PET sequentially.
source: The homologous C-termini of Reh1 and Rei1 occupy the PET sequentially (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The departure of Rei1 seems to be concurrent with Arx1 release.
source: While the departure of Rei1 seems to be concurrent with Arx1 release, the C-terminus of Reh1 unexpectedly persists in the exit tunnel even after the departure of Nmd3 and Lsg1.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing the presence of Reh1 in state VI.

claim: The C-terminus of Reh1 unexpectedly persists in the exit tunnel even after the departure of Nmd3 and Lsg1.
source: While the departure of Rei1 seems to be concurrent with Arx1 release, the C-terminus of Reh1 unexpectedly persists in the exit tunnel even after the departure of Nmd3 and Lsg1.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing the presence of Reh1 in state VI.

claim: The timing of the exchange of Rei1 for Reh1 (between states I-II) is consistent with XL-MS analysis that yielded crosslinks between Rei1, Arx1 and eL24, while Reh1 yielded crosslinks to eL24, but not to Rei1 or Arx1.
source: The timing of the exchange of Rei1 for Reh1 (between states I-II) is consistent with XL-MS analysis that yielded crosslinks between Rei1, Arx1 and eL24, while Reh1 yielded crosslinks to eL24, but not to Rei1 or Arx1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: The exchange of Reh1 for Rei1 occurs at the time of Arx1 release.
source: We conclude that the exchange of Reh1 for Rei1 occurs at the time of Arx1 release, but that surveillance of the PET by Reh1 continues throughout the entire process of cytoplasmic pre-60S maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and XL-MS data.

claim: Surveillance of the PET by Reh1 continues throughout the entire process of cytoplasmic pre-60S maturation.
source: We conclude that the exchange of Reh1 for Rei1 occurs at the time of Arx1 release, but that surveillance of the PET by Reh1 continues throughout the entire process of cytoplasmic pre-60S maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing Reh1 persistence.

claim: The N-termini of both Rei1 and Reh1 extend up across the surface of eL24 to directly interact with eIF6 subdomains C and D and with a loop that extends out from the α-helical domain of Lsg1 (residues G438-T456).
source: While the overall structures of Rei1 and Reh1 are consistent with previous reports (Greber et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2017), our maps reveal additional density that corresponds to the N-termini of both Rei1 and Reh1 extending up across the surface of eL24 to directly interact with eIF6 subdomains C and D and with a loop that extends out from the α-helical domain of Lsg1 (residues G438-T456) (Figure 1A, state I).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 1A, state I.

claim: The Lsg1 α-helical domain (residues G474-D479) interacts with uL14.
source: The Lsg1 α-helical domain (residues G474-D479) also interacts with uL14.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The position of the extreme C-terminal leucine and glutamine residues of Rei1 and Reh1 differs compared with previous reports.
source: Interestingly, the position of the extreme C-terminal leucine and glutamine residues of Rei1 and Reh1 differs compared with previous reports (Ma et al., 2017; Greber et al., 2016): the side chains of Q393 (Rei1) and Q432 (Reh1) form an electrostatic interaction with the base of U2875 (H89), while the backbone interacts with the base of U2978 (H93).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: The side chains of Q393 (Rei1) and Q432 (Reh1) form an electrostatic interaction with the base of U2875 (H89), while the backbone interacts with the base of U2978 (H93).
source: Interestingly, the position of the extreme C-terminal leucine and glutamine residues of Rei1 and Reh1 differs compared with previous reports (Ma et al., 2017; Greber et al., 2016): the side chains of Q393 (Rei1) and Q432 (Reh1) form an electrostatic interaction with the base of U2875 (H89), while the backbone interacts with the base of U2978 (H93).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing specific interactions.

claim: The coexistence of eIF6 and Reh1 on the same particle suggests that state VI is not simply a product of eIF6 rebinding but is a bona fide late pre-60S subunit maturation intermediate that lies downstream of Nmd3 and Lsg1 release.
source: The coexistence of eIF6 and Reh1 on the same particle (Figure 1B) suggests that state VI is not simply a product of eIF6 rebinding but is a bona fide late pre-60S subunit maturation intermediate that lies downstream of Nmd3 and Lsg1 release.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing coexistence of eIF6 and Reh1.

claim: State VI supports the hypothesis that eIF6 is evicted after Nmd3.
source: These data support the hypothesis that eIF6 is evicted after Nmd3 (Weis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Nmd3 extends across the entire tRNA binding cleft on the intersubunit face of the 60S subunit from uL1 at the L1 stalk through the E, P and A sites to contact Lsg1 and eIF6 at the SRL.
source: Nmd3 extends across the entire tRNA binding cleft on the intersubunit face of the 60S subunit from uL1 at the L1 stalk through the E, P and A sites to contact Lsg1 and eIF6 at the SRL (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The cryo-EM density allowed building a complete atomic model for Nmd3 (residues T16-R404) including backbone atoms and side chains.
source: The cryo-EM density allowed us to build a complete atomic model for Nmd3 (residues T16-R404) including backbone atoms and side chains (Figure 2A), revealing a multi-domain architecture that includes two treble clef zinc fingers (that superimpose with an RMSD of 1 Å over 13 Cα atoms; Figure 2A, inset), two alpha-beta domains and two beta-barrel domains.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density and the atomic model shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nmd3 has a multi-domain architecture that includes two treble clef zinc fingers, two alpha-beta domains and two beta-barrel domains.
source: The cryo-EM density allowed us to build a complete atomic model for Nmd3 (residues T16-R404) including backbone atoms and side chains (Figure 2A), revealing a multi-domain architecture that includes two treble clef zinc fingers (that superimpose with an RMSD of 1 Å over 13 Cα atoms; Figure 2A, inset), two alpha-beta domains and two beta-barrel domains.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The two treble clef zinc fingers of Nmd3 superimpose with an RMSD of 1 Å over 13 Cα atoms.
source: The cryo-EM density allowed us to build a complete atomic model for Nmd3 (residues T16-R404) including backbone atoms and side chains (Figure 2A), revealing a multi-domain architecture that includes two treble clef zinc fingers (that superimpose with an RMSD of 1 Å over 13 Cα atoms; Figure 2A, inset), two alpha-beta domains and two beta-barrel domains.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 2A, inset.

claim: The N-terminal treble clef zinc finger (residues 16–42, C19-C22-C35-C38) is grafted into an alpha-beta domain (residues 43–154) that is structurally related to ribosomal protein eL31.
source: The N-terminal treble clef zinc finger (residues 16–42, C19-C22-C35-C38) is grafted into an alpha-beta domain (residues 43–154) that is structurally related to ribosomal protein eL31.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The second alpha-beta domain (residues 155–250) is structurally related to ribosomal protein eL22.
source: The second alpha-beta domain (residues 155–250) is structurally related to ribosomal protein eL22, while the two C-terminal beta-barrel domains have SH3 (251–310) and OB (311-400) folds, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The two C-terminal beta-barrel domains of Nmd3 have SH3 (251–310) and OB (311-400) folds.
source: The second alpha-beta domain (residues 155–250) is structurally related to ribosomal protein eL22, while the two C-terminal beta-barrel domains have SH3 (251–310) and OB (311-400) folds, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The combination of the SH3 and OB domains is similar in sequence and structure to eIF-5A-1, but the domains are oriented differently with respect to each other.
source: Although the combination of the SH3 and OB domains is similar in sequence and structure to eIF-5A-1, the domains are oriented differently with respect to each other.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Nmd3 comprises a modular assembly of existing structural blocks associated with the ribosomal machinery combined together to form a functionally distinct protein.
source: Thus, Nmd3 comprises a modular assembly of existing structural blocks associated with the ribosomal machinery combined together to form a functionally distinct protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis showing similarity to ribosomal proteins.

claim: The Nmd3 OB domain holds the L1 stalk in the closed position.
source: The Nmd3 OB domain holds the L1 stalk in the closed position, while the eL22-like, SH3 and OB domains, together with an extended C-terminal loop, encircle and distort the tip of H38 (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The eL22-like, SH3 and OB domains of Nmd3, together with an extended C-terminal loop, encircle and distort the tip of H38.
source: The Nmd3 OB domain holds the L1 stalk in the closed position, while the eL22-like, SH3 and OB domains, together with an extended C-terminal loop, encircle and distort the tip of H38 (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Two loops (β1–2 and β3–4) from the OB domain stabilize a base-flip of A1025.
source: Specifically, two loops (β1–2 and β3–4) from the OB domain stabilize a base-flip of A1025.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The side chain and backbone atoms of N332 contact the base and backbone phosphate of A1025.
source: The side chain and backbone atoms of N332 contact the base and backbone phosphate of A1025.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: H364 contacts the backbone phosphate of A1027.
source: H364 contacts the backbone phosphate of A1027, while the side chains of Y402 and R404 contact the backbone phosphates of A1026-G1029.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The side chains of Y402 and R404 contact the backbone phosphates of A1026-G1029.
source: H364 contacts the backbone phosphate of A1027, while the side chains of Y402 and R404 contact the backbone phosphates of A1026-G1029.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: Within the SH3 domain, the side chain of K253 contacts the phosphate backbone of C1023.
source: Within the SH3 domain, the side chain of K253 contacts the phosphate backbone of C1023.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: Helix α1 from the eL22-like domain (particularly the side chains of R169 and Q176) packs against the bases and backbone of H38 (G1020-C1023).
source: Helix α1 from the eL22-like domain (particularly the side chains of R169 and Q176) packs against the bases and backbone of H38 (G1020-C1023).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: Throughout the steps of pre-60S subunit maturation visualised, H69 adopts a conformation that differs from the mature ribosome but that surprisingly persists even in the absence of Nmd3 and Lsg1 (state VI).
source: Throughout the steps of pre-60S subunit maturation visualised herein, H69 adopts a conformation that differs from the mature ribosome (Ben-Shem et al., 2011) but that surprisingly persists even in the absence of Nmd3 and Lsg1 (state VI) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Lsg1 stabilises a base flip at G2261 (H69).
source: Lsg1 stabilises a base flip at G2261 (H69) (Figure 3A), while the side chain of Lsg1 W142 stacks against the base of A2256 at the tip of H69 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The side chain of Lsg1 W142 stacks against the base of A2256 at the tip of H69.
source: Lsg1 stabilises a base flip at G2261 (H69) (Figure 3A), while the side chain of Lsg1 W142 stacks against the base of A2256 at the tip of H69 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A β-hairpin in the SH3 domain of Nmd3 stabilises a base flip in U2269 at the junction between H68 and H69.
source: The altered conformation of H69 is also promoted by a β-hairpin in the SH3 domain of Nmd3 that stabilises a base flip in U2269 at the junction between H68 and H69 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Nmd3 SH3 domain makes additional interactions with the 25S rRNA using two short α-helices (SH3-α1 and SH3-α2).
source: The Nmd3 SH3 domain makes additional interactions with the 25S rRNA using two short α-helices (SH3-α1 and SH3-α2) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: H69 may only adopt the mature conformation after joining of the 60S and 40S subunits.
source: As the altered conformation of H69 is maintained even in the absence of both Nmd3 and Lsg1 (state VI), we suggest that H69 may only adopt the mature conformation after joining of the 60S and 40S subunits.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that H69 remains in an altered conformation in state VI.

claim: Compared with the reconstituted Nmd3-Lsg1-60S particle, the Nmd3 eL31-like domain is rotated (60°) away from H89 towards the long α-helix of the Lsg1 GTPase domain in each of the native intermediates carrying Lsg1 and Nmd3 (states I-V).
source: Compared with the reconstituted Nmd3-Lsg1-60S particle (Malyutin et al., 2017), the Nmd3 eL31-like domain is rotated (60°) away from H89 towards the long α-helix of the Lsg1 GTPase domain in each of the native intermediates carrying Lsg1 and Nmd3 (states I-V) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a previous structure.

claim: The interaction between the Nmd3 eL31-like domain and Lsg1 involves a stacking interaction between the side chain of Nmd3 residue W104 and the side chain of Lsg1 residue R163.
source: The interaction involves a stacking interaction between the side chain of Nmd3 residue W104 and the side chain of Lsg1 residue R163 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Heteronuclear 1H {15N} NOE analysis of the Archaeoglobus fulgidus Nmd3 (residues 22–150) indicates that the N-terminal zinc finger (residues 22–43) has a higher degree of motion than the attached eL31 domain on the picosecond timescale.
source: Heteronuclear 1H {15N} NOE analysis of the Archaeoglobus fulgidus Nmd3 (residues 22–150) indicates that the N-terminal zinc finger (residues 22–43) has a higher degree of motion than the attached eL31 domain on the picosecond timescale (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Exchange broadened residues indicate the presence of a flexible linker between the N-terminal zinc finger and eL31 domain that is undergoing segmental motion.
source: Exchange broadened residues indicate the presence of a flexible linker between the two domains that is undergoing segmental motion.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data.

claim: The Nmd3 N-terminal zinc finger has dynamic mobility that allows it to sample a range of positions in solution.
source: These data indicate that the Nmd3 N-terminal zinc finger has dynamic mobility that allows it to sample a range of positions in solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data.

claim: The Nmd3 zinc finger remains bound to eIF6 subdomains D and E throughout states I-V.
source: However, the cryo-EM data indicate that the Nmd3 zinc finger remains bound to eIF6 subdomains D and E (total buried surface area of 107 Å2) throughout states I-V (Figure 3F), providing a click-lock that fixes the Nmd3 N-terminus in position throughout pre-60S maturation.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The binding of the Nmd3 zinc finger to eIF6 provides a click-lock that fixes the Nmd3 N-terminus in position throughout pre-60S maturation.
source: However, the cryo-EM data indicate that the Nmd3 zinc finger remains bound to eIF6 subdomains D and E (total buried surface area of 107 Å2) throughout states I-V (Figure 3F), providing a click-lock that fixes the Nmd3 N-terminus in position throughout pre-60S maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: In the late nuclear pre-60S particle purified using epitope-tagged Nog2, the N-terminal domain of Nog1 separates H89 into two strands, H89 adopting an upright position.
source: In the late nuclear pre-60S particle purified using epitope-tagged Nog2, the N-terminal domain of Nog1 separates H89 into two strands, H89 adopting an upright position (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the absence of eL40 (states I-II), H89 adopts a range of conformations even with Yvh1 present.
source: Focused classification around the H89 density revealed that in the absence of eL40 (states I-II), H89 adopts a range of conformations even with Yvh1 present (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Following the departure of Yvh1, eL40 stabilises H89 in its near-mature conformation by forming two major contacts with the opposing H91, including a stacking interaction of A2847 (H89) with G2898 (H91) and base pairing between C2844 (H89) and G2898 (H91).
source: However, following the departure of Yvh1, eL40 stabilises H89 in its near-mature conformation by forming two major contacts with the opposing H91, including a stacking interaction of A2847 (H89) with G2898 (H91) and base pairing between C2844 (H89) and G2898 (H91) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: An observed contact between Yvh1 and the side chain of uL6 K141 overlaps with the binding site for the N-terminus of eL40 in state III.
source: An observed contact between Yvh1 and the side chain of uL6 K141 overlaps with the binding site for the N-terminus of eL40 in state III, raising the possibility that the recruitment of eL40 may destabilise Yvh1 to promote its departure from the pre-60S particle.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The recruitment of eL40 may destabilise Yvh1 to promote its departure from the pre-60S particle.
source: An observed contact between Yvh1 and the side chain of uL6 K141 overlaps with the binding site for the N-terminus of eL40 in state III, raising the possibility that the recruitment of eL40 may destabilise Yvh1 to promote its departure from the pre-60S particle.
evidence: This is speculated based on the overlapping binding sites.

claim: The docking of uL16 to the upper surface of H89 promotes a dramatic ~65° rotation of H38 away from Nmd3.
source: In turn, the docking of uL16 to the upper surface of H89 promotes a dramatic ~65° rotation of H38 away from Nmd3 (Figure 4C), sandwiching uL16 in a cleft between H38 and H89 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: uL16 is sandwiched in a cleft between H38 and H89.
source: In turn, the docking of uL16 to the upper surface of H89 promotes a dramatic ~65° rotation of H38 away from Nmd3 (Figure 4C), sandwiching uL16 in a cleft between H38 and H89 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In mature, actively translating ribosomes with tRNA bound, the eukaryotic-specific loop (residues 102–112) of uL16 extends into the PTC.
source: In mature, actively translating ribosomes with tRNA bound, the eukaryotic-specific loop (residues 102–112) of uL16 extends into the PTC (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In states I-IV the eL22-like domain of Nmd3 extends into the PTC where it is surrounded by helices H64, H69-71, H80, H90 and H92-93.
source: However, in states I-IV the eL22-like domain of Nmd3 extends into the PTC where it is surrounded by helices H64, H69-71, H80, H90 and H92-93 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Residues on the surface of the eL22-like domain β-sheet make extensive interactions with the backbone of H80.
source: Residues on the surface of the eL22-like domain β-sheet make extensive interactions with the backbone of H80 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Residue N205 (α2 helix) stabilises a stacking base pair interaction between C2308 (H64) and C2284 (H70).
source: Residue N205 (α2 helix) stabilises a stacking base pair interaction between C2308 (H64) and C2284 (H70) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The β4–5 loop of Nmd3 stabilises the 'closed' conformation of base A2971 through specific interactions with the side chains of K204 (helix α2), K224, F242 (strand β5), Y240 and the backbone amide of S238 (β4–5 loop).
source: Furthermore, the β4–5 loop of Nmd3 stabilises the 'closed' conformation of base A2971 through specific interactions with the side chains of K204 (helix α2), K224, F242 (strand β5), Y240 and the backbone amide of S238 (β4–5 loop) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The uL16 P-site loop is unable to extend into the PTC in state IV because of a steric clash with the Nmd3 β4–5 hairpin loop.
source: As a result, the uL16 P-site loop is unable to extend into the PTC in state IV because of a steric clash with the Nmd3 β4–5 hairpin loop.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing overlapping binding sites.

claim: The initial docking of uL16 is fully compatible with retention of Nmd3 on the pre-60S particle.
source: The initial docking of uL16 is fully compatible with retention of Nmd3 on the pre-60S particle (Figure 1A, Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A, Figure 6A,B.

claim: uL16 liberates H38 from the C-terminus of Nmd3 promoting partial (20°) (state V) and subsequently full (56°) retraction (state VI) of the L1 stalk.
source: However, uL16 liberates H38 from the C-terminus of Nmd3 promoting partial (20°) (state V) and subsequently full (56°) retraction (state VI) of the L1 stalk (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Partial retraction of the L1 stalk (state V) is accompanied by a conformational switch in Nmd3 in which the OB, SH3 and eL22-like domains are displaced upwards and outwards from the P and E sites by ~20 Å through a pivot point between the flexible helical linker connecting the eL22- and eL31-like domains.
source: Partial retraction of the L1 stalk (state V) is accompanied by a conformational switch in Nmd3 in which the OB, SH3 and eL22-like domains are displaced upwards and outwards from the P and E sites by ~20 Å through a pivot point between the flexible helical linker connecting the eL22- and eL31-like domains, while the N-terminus remains anchored to eIF6 and Lsg1 (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: During the conformational switch in Nmd3, the N-terminus remains anchored to eIF6 and Lsg1.
source: Partial retraction of the L1 stalk (state V) is accompanied by a conformational switch in Nmd3 in which the OB, SH3 and eL22-like domains are displaced upwards and outwards from the P and E sites by ~20 Å through a pivot point between the flexible helical linker connecting the eL22- and eL31-like domains, while the N-terminus remains anchored to eIF6 and Lsg1 (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: Displacement of the eL22-like domain breaks the interaction of residue N205 (helix α2) with C2308 (H64) and C2284 (H70).
source: Displacement of the eL22-like domain breaks the interaction of residue N205 (helix α2) with C2308 (H64) and C2284 (H70) (Figure 5C), allowing helix α2 to form a new contact with H69 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Displacement of the eL22-like domain allows helix α2 to form a new contact with H69.
source: Displacement of the eL22-like domain breaks the interaction of residue N205 (helix α2) with C2308 (H64) and C2284 (H70) (Figure 5C), allowing helix α2 to form a new contact with H69 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Displacement of the β4–5 hairpin loop from the entrance to the PTC (state V) permits the uL16 P-site loop to extend into the PTC where the highly conserved, essential residue R110 coordinates A2971 in an 'open' flipped-up conformation.
source: Displacement of the β4–5 hairpin loop from the entrance to the PTC (state V) permits the uL16 P-site loop to extend into the PTC where the highly conserved, essential residue R110 coordinates A2971 in an 'open' flipped-up conformation (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Genetic and biochemical analysis are consistent with an essential role for the uL16 P-site loop in Nmd3 release.
source: Genetic and biochemical analysis are consistent with an essential role for the uL16 P-site loop in Nmd3 release (Hofer et al., 2007; Bussiere et al., 2012; Sulima et al., 2014; Weis et al., 2015; Patchett et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An nmd3-N205D allele rescued the fitness defect of yeast cells expressing the T-ALL-associated uL16-R98S mutant as the sole copy of uL16.
source: Furthermore, an nmd3-N205D allele rescued the fitness defect of yeast cells expressing the T-ALL-associated uL16-R98S mutant as the sole copy of uL16 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic complementation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The uL16 P-site loop drives the conformational equilibrium in favour of Nmd3 release by competing with Nmd3 for an overlapping binding site within the PTC.
source: We conclude that the uL16 P-site loop drives the conformational equilibrium in favour of Nmd3 release by competing with Nmd3 for an overlapping binding site within the PTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and genetic data.

claim: The C-terminus of Reh1 is retained in the PET in a late assembly intermediate carrying eIF6 that is downstream of Lsg1 and Nmd3 release (state VI).
source: Unexpectedly, our data reveal that the C-terminus of Reh1 is retained in the PET in a late assembly intermediate carrying eIF6 that is downstream of Lsg1 and Nmd3 release (state VI) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Identification of state VI provides compelling evidence that eIF6 release by SBDS and EFL1 occurs after the dissociation of Nmd3 and Lsg1.
source: Identification of this particle provides compelling evidence that eIF6 release by SBDS and EFL1 occurs after the dissociation of Nmd3 and Lsg1 as proposed (Weis et al., 2015) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The binding sites for SBDS, Nmd3 and Lsg1 are incompatible, precluding the removal of eIF6 before the departure of Lsg1 and Nmd3.
source: Importantly, we also note that the binding sites for SBDS, Nmd3 and Lsg1 are incompatible, precluding the removal of eIF6 before the departure of Lsg1 and Nmd3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Lsg1 and Nmd3 function at least in part as placeholders for SBDS.
source: We conclude that Nmd3 and Lsg1 are released prior to SBDS and EFL1 recruitment and that Lsg1 and Nmd3 function at least in part as placeholders for SBDS.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing incompatible binding sites.

claim: SBDS and EFL1 interrogate the structural and functional integrity of the completed PTC by licensing removal of the anti-association factor eIF6.
source: This study reinforces the concept that SBDS and EFL1 interrogate the structural and functional integrity of the completed PTC by licensing removal of the anti-association factor eIF6 (Weis et al., 2015) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The side chain of SBDS residue R11 and the backbone of K62 interact with the side chain of R110 within the uL16 P-site loop that stabilises the flipped-out conformation of base A2971.
source: The side chain of SBDS residue R11 and the backbone of K62 interact with the side chain of R110 within the uL16 P-site loop that stabilises the flipped-out conformation of base A2971 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There are interesting parallels between the interactions of the uL16 P-site loop with the N-terminus of SBDS and the contacts of uL16 with the P-site tRNA during decoding.
source: In addition, there are interesting parallels between the interactions of the uL16 P-site loop with the N-terminus of SBDS (pdb 6qkl) (Weis et al., 2015) and the contacts of uL16 with the P-site tRNA during decoding (pdb 5gak) (Schmidt et al., 2016) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The PET of the large ribosomal subunit appears to be directly monitored initially in the nucleus by Nog1 and subsequently throughout the entire process of cytoplasmic assembly by Rei1 and Reh1 in turn.
source: The PET of the large ribosomal subunit appears to be directly monitored initially in the nucleus by Nog1 (Wu et al., 2016) and subsequently throughout the entire process of cytoplasmic assembly by Rei1 (Greber et al., 2012; Greber et al., 2016) and Reh1 (Ma et al., 2017) in turn.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The direct interaction between the α-helical domain of Lsg1 and the N-termini of both Rei1 and Reh1 suggests how events at the PET and PTC might be coupled during cytoplasmic maturation.
source: Indeed, the direct interaction between the α-helical domain of Lsg1 and the N-termini of both Rei1 and Reh1 (Figure 1A) suggests how events at the PET and PTC might be coupled during cytoplasmic maturation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural data.

claim: The C-terminus of Reh1 may interact directly with the N-terminus of SBDS during late 60S maturation.
source: Docking analysis raises the possibility that the C-terminus of Reh1 may interact directly with the N-terminus of SBDS during late 60S maturation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is speculated based on docking analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The uL16-R98S mutation may increase the flexibility of the P-site loop, reducing its ability to effectively compete with the Nmd3 eL22-like domain for the overlapping binding site at base A2971 in the PTC.
source: We propose that the uL16-R98S mutation may increase the flexibility of the P-site loop, reducing its ability to effectively compete with the Nmd3 eL22-like domain for the overlapping binding site at base A2971 in the PTC, thereby driving the equilibrium towards Nmd3 release.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural data and the location of the mutation.

claim: Coupling of the flipped-out base G2261 in H69 to the Lsg1 Switch one region may regulate Lsg1 GTP hydrolysis.
source: It has been proposed that coupling of the flipped-out base G2261 in H69 to the Lsg1 Switch one region (that coordinates a magnesium ion in the active site) may regulate Lsg1 GTP hydrolysis (Malyutin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study.

claim: The G2261 base-flip appears to persist throughout all the stages of cytoplasmic 60S maturation visualised, even in the absence of Lsg1.
source: However, the G2261 base-flip appears to persist throughout all the stages of cytoplasmic 60S maturation visualised, even in the absence of Lsg1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Nmd3 eL22-like domain establishes a new contact with H69 as the L1 stalk retracts.
source: By contrast, the Nmd3 eL22-like domain establishes a new contact with H69 as the L1 stalk retracts (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction of Nmd3 with H69 may transiently reposition base G2261, thereby relaying the change in conformation to the Switch one region to activate Lsg1 GTP hydrolysis.
source: We speculate that this interaction of Nmd3 with H69 may transiently reposition base G2261, thereby relaying the change in conformation to the Switch one region to activate Lsg1 GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural data.

claim: A crosslink was identified between the N-terminus of Lsg1 and the P-site loop of uL16.
source: The identification of a crosslink between the N-terminus of Lsg1 and the P-site loop of uL16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B and Supplementary file 2) raises the intriguing possibility that Lsg1 may proofread accommodation of the uL16 P-site loop into the PTC as the Nmd3 β4–5 loop is retracted.
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: Lsg1 may proofread accommodation of the uL16 P-site loop into the PTC as the Nmd3 β4–5 loop is retracted.
source: The identification of a crosslink between the N-terminus of Lsg1 and the P-site loop of uL16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B and Supplementary file 2) raises the intriguing possibility that Lsg1 may proofread accommodation of the uL16 P-site loop into the PTC as the Nmd3 β4–5 loop is retracted.
evidence: This is speculated based on the XL-MS data.

claim: Lsg1 may act as a gatekeeper that licenses further progression of 60S subunit maturation by dissociating only once it senses that uL16 is correctly integrated.
source: In this model, Lsg1 may act as a gatekeeper that licenses further progression of 60S subunit maturation by dissociating only once it senses that uL16 is correctly integrated.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural and XL-MS data.

claim: The disengagement of Lsg1 from the N-terminus of Nmd3 will further destabilise the interaction of Nmd3 with the 60S subunit, allowing retraction of the L1 stalk to pull Nmd3 completely off the intersubunit face.
source: The disengagement of Lsg1 from the N-terminus of Nmd3 will further destabilise the interaction of Nmd3 with the 60S subunit, allowing retraction of the L1 stalk to pull Nmd3 completely off the intersubunit face.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural data.

claim: The cryo-EM data provide a mechanistic model that allows interpretation of the consequences of the recurrent uL16-R98S mutation found in paediatric T-ALL.
source: Importantly, given the high degree of conservation in the amino acid sequence and structure of the uL16 protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), our cryo-EM data provide a mechanistic model that allows us to interpret the consequences of the recurrent uL16-R98S mutation found in paediatric T-ALL (De Keersmaecker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and the conservation of uL16.

claim: Yvh1 dissociates from the pre-60S particle prior to the binding of eL40 and uL16.
source: Our study suggests that Yvh1 dissociates from the pre-60S particle prior to the binding of eL40 and uL16 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Yvh1 was reported to bind cytoplasmic pre-60S particles carrying eL40 and uL16.
source: However, while this work was under review, Yvh1 was reported to bind cytoplasmic pre-60S particles carrying eL40 and uL16 (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from another study.

claim: The discrepancy between this study and Zhou et al. may be explained by the fact that this study exclusively analysed native pre-60S particles, while Zhou et al examined particles purified from Rlp24-mutant cells or following treatment with the inhibitor diazaborine.
source: Perhaps explaining this discrepancy, our study has exclusively analysed native pre-60S particles, while Zhou et al examined particles purified from Rlp24-mutant cells or following treatment with the inhibitor diazaborine (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an explanation for the discrepancy based on differences in experimental approaches.
